performers: Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, soprano; Philharmonia Orchestra; Otto Ackermann
intro: “Im Abendrot”, marked Andante, is the fourth of Strauss’s Four Last Songs; an old couple watch the evening fade, and at the closing question Strauss quoted a melody he had written nearly sixty years earlier. Elisabeth Schwarzkopf sings the complete song with Otto Ackermann and the Philharmonia Orchestra in their 1953 recording.

cues.title: Orchestral prelude
cues.text: The violins play a long descending line above held brass chords and a deep E♭. Woodwinds double and decorate the melody. The soprano rests through this Andante prelude and does not enter until after rehearsal B.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score (1950), plate B. & H. 16918, pp. 44–46: Andante orchestral prelude, with the voice resting until after rehearsal B. https://petruccimusiclibrary.ca/files/imglnks/caimg/8/83/IMSLP615036-PMLP36684-Strauss_-_Four_Last_Songs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First stanza, soprano
cues.text: Eichendorff’s couple has travelled together through hardship and happiness. The soprano sings their story in a moving line over short phrases in the strings, which keep a walking pace beneath her.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score (1950), pp. 46–48, first stanza after rehearsal B; Joseph von Eichendorff’s German text is also printed in the original Angel 35084 booklet. https://archive.org/download/lp_four-last-songs-capriccio-op-85-closing_richard-strauss-elisabeth-schwarzkopf-phil/lp_four-last-songs-capriccio-op-85-closing_richard-strauss-elisabeth-schwarzkopf-phil_djvu.txt
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Montreux, May 1948
cues.text: Strauss finished Im Abendrot at Montreux on 6 May 1948, a month before his eighty-fourth birthday. It was the first of the four songs to be completed. After his death the publisher Ernst Roth placed it last and gave the collection its title.
cues.evidence: Bryan Gilliam’s Boston Symphony programme note quotes Ernst Roth’s account of the manuscript dates and describes Roth’s posthumous title and ordering. https://www.bso.org/works/four-last-songs

cues.title: Larks, two flutes
cues.text: The poem has two larks rising above the darkening valleys. Strauss gives them to a pair of flutes, which trill above the soprano and the sustained strings.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score (1950), pp. 49–51, rehearsals D–E: the paired flute trills surround the second stanza’s larks and continue into the third stanza. Calvin Dotsey’s Houston Symphony note describes the word painting: https://houstonsymphony.org/strauss-four-last-songs/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quotation from Tod und Verklärung
cues.text: After the final vocal question about death, the orchestra brings back the transfiguration theme from Tod und Verklärung, completed in 1889. The soprano’s part ends and the orchestra continues into a long postlude.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score (1950), pp. 53–55, rehearsals G–I, and Andrew Porter’s Angel 35084 booklet identify the quotation around the final vocal question. The earlier work’s completion in 1889 is documented by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/strausss-death-transfiguration/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piccolo trills and final chord
cues.text: The two flautists change to piccolos for the final bird calls. Their trills sound above the orchestra as the tempo slows, and the song ends on an E♭ major chord.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score (1950), p. 55, rehearsal I: both flute parts change to piccolo; rit. sehr langsam and the final E♭ major chord. https://petruccimusiclibrary.ca/files/imglnks/caimg/8/83/IMSLP615036-PMLP36684-Strauss_-_Four_Last_Songs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Elisabeth Schwarzkopf (soprano), Philharmonia Orchestra (orchestra), Otto Ackermann (conductor)
fields.note: All three credits appear on the original side-one label. The consulted sources do not identify the individual orchestral soloists. This is the Ackermann recording, distinct from Schwarzkopf’s later recording with George Szell.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Complete song in the original scoring for soprano and orchestra, sung in German
fields.note: The fourth song is separately banded on the LP and transferred as one complete track. The published score places the orchestral prelude on pp. 44–46, the vocal stanzas on pp. 46–54, and the postlude on pp. 54–55. Hall sections and musical cues use approximate score-proportion passage timings; no bar alignment or syllable-level timing is asserted. The edition of the orchestral parts used at the session is unknown.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Warner’s reissue metadata, reproduced by Presto, dates the Four Last Songs to 25 September 1953 and the accompanying Capriccio scene to 26 September. Naxos gives 25–26 September for the songs. Month-level precision retains the date on which both accounts agree; the exact day and take of Im Abendrot remain unresolved.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The Warner track documentation names Watford Town Hall. The original Angel label states Recorded in England.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable with Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; whole-side 24-bit FLAC transfer and segmented VBR MP3 access derivative

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Strauss’s music and Eichendorff’s German poem are public domain under ordinary EU life-plus-70 terms.
fields.note: Strauss died in 1949 and Eichendorff in 1857. This assessment concerns Im Abendrot alone, not the three other songs’ Hermann Hesse texts. The score was first published in 1950 and remains identified by IMSLP as protected in the United States; no US composition clearance is asserted. The copyrighted English translation in the LP booklet is not reproduced.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public domain under the pre-1963 commercial-publication rule: Angel 35084 was published in 1954.
fields.note: The documented 1954 lawful commercial issue predates the programme’s 1963 cutoff. Its former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013. This is a territorial term assessment, not a Creative Commons licence or a declaration of US or worldwide public-domain status. The transferred LP, not a modern commercial remaster, supplies the audio.

composer.epithet: Composer, the son of a horn player, who wrote long farewell songs for soprano.
facts: Munich, with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer; conducting with Hans von Bülow at Meiningen
Munich · Weimar · Berlin Court Opera, 1898–1918 · Vienna State Opera, 1919–24
Tone poems, fifteen operas, two horn concertos and more than two hundred songs
composer.background:
Richard Strauss grew up hearing the horn. His father Franz played in the Munich Court Orchestra, including the first performances of Wagner’s Tristan and Die Meistersinger, and detested the music. At home, Mozart was placed above every other composer, and Haydn and Beethoven were also approved. Richard, born in 1864, had piano lessons from the age of four and was composing at six. His mother Josepha came from the Pschorr brewing family. He studied privately with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer and learnt how an orchestra sounds from the players who worked beside his father.

Hans von Bülow took him to Meiningen in 1885. At twenty-one he had an orchestra of his own to rehearse, as well as a choir and a princess to teach. The violinist Alexander Ritter, married to Wagner’s niece, completed his conversion to the music his father disliked. Ritter also urged Liszt’s symphonic poems upon him. Strauss spent the next decade writing for the concert orchestra without voices.
